speed.intro: Control crawl throughput. Increasing parallelism speeds the crawl, but every extra request adds load on the target server — pick numbers a host that you don't own can absorb without rate-limiting / 429s.
speed.adaptiveSpeedHint: Only affects behaviour when the server pushes back — a healthy site is crawled at the full ceiling either way.

speed.ceilingEmpty: Set Max Concurrency and Max RPS to see the projected throughput.
speed.worstCaseDelay: Worst-case delay per failed URL ≈ initialDelay × (2 ^ attempts − 1) = {{value}}
speed.tip1: For a quick first sweep on a healthy site try the <bold>Fast</bold> preset (Settings → Presets) — concurrency 40, RPS 40, no retries.
speed.tip2: For unreliable origins or slow APIs try <bold>Thorough</bold> — concurrency 10, 3 retries, 30 s timeout.
speed.tip3: Concurrency × HTTP keep-alive = the steady-state connection count. Most servers comfortably handle 20–40; corporate proxies / WAFs often cap at 8–10.

auth.intro: HTTP authentication applied on every request. Useful for staging environments behind Basic/Digest auth, or APIs that require a Bearer token. For sites behind an HTML login form, use Form Login below instead.

formLogin.intro: Steps run in order over one shared cookie jar. A GET step can capture a CSRF token from the page; a POST step submits credentials (and the captured token) as a form. Reference captured values with {{name}}.

duplicates.intro: Near-duplicate detection. After every crawl, body text is hashed with a 64-bit SimHash, and pages whose hashes lie within the configured Hamming distance of each other are clustered as near-duplicates. Surfaced under
duplicates.maxHamming: Max Hamming distance (0 = exact only, 12 = very loose, 0 disables)
duplicates.thresholdHint: Lower = stricter. 3 is the SF-equivalent default. Pages with too little body content (<50 characters) are excluded from clustering regardless of threshold.
duplicates.similarityHint: Pages whose main-content wording is at least this similar are clustered too — this catches rewritten or lightly edited copies that SimHash misses. 90 is the SF-equivalent default.
duplicates.costBody: SimHash adds ~5-10 ms per page during crawl; clustering itself runs after the last URL completes (~3-10 s at 1M URLs, <500 ms at 100K).

hardware.intro: Resource caps for the crawler process. Useful for keeping the machine usable while crawling large sites (1M+ URLs).
hardware.memoryHint: When the crawler's RSS exceeds this, the queue auto-pauses and resumes once memory drops below 80% of the cap. Soft cap — does not enforce a hard heap limit.
hardware.queueHint: Hard cap on pending URLs held in memory. Excess discoveries are dropped silently — bounds peak heap during fan-out bursts (large sitemaps, dense link graphs). Set conservatively if memory is tight.
hardware.priorityHint1: OS scheduler hint. Lowering priority lets the rest of the machine stay responsive during heavy crawls. Effective on next crawl start; may require elevated privileges on some platforms. For raw CPU concurrency, see

crawlAnalysis.intro: Per-pass post-crawl analysis toggles. Each pass runs after the HTTP fetch phase finishes and feeds different issue filters. Skip passes you don't need to shave wall-clock on large crawls; the related issue counters quietly read as 0 until the pass runs.

issues.intro: Turn individual issue checks off for this project — for example "Description = Title" on a CMS that does it on purpose.
issues.effect: A disabled check disappears from the sidebar, the overview counts, HTML/PDF reports, bulk export and the crawl-complete webhook. Nothing is deleted — turn it back on to see its results again.

advanced.intro: Lower-level caps and link-follow toggles. Defaults are tuned for typical SEO audits — only touch these if you know why.

cookies.intro: Cookie policy applied to every fetch. The crawler is otherwise stateless across requests; this setting controls whether Set-Cookie response headers are recorded for the cookie-flag issue checks (Missing Secure / HttpOnly / SameSite).
cookies.valuesNeverStored2: stored in the project file regardless of this setting — only the security flag (Secure / HttpOnly / SameSite) counts are kept.

rendering.intro: JavaScript rendering uses headless Chromium (Playwright) to fetch the post-load DOM after scripts execute. Required for SPA / hydration-only content. Significantly slower than text mode — every URL pays a browser-launch and wait cost. Enable in the Crawler panel under Rendering Mode.
rendering.disabledHint: Rendering Mode is currently set to Text or Old AJAX. Switch to JavaScript Rendering in the Crawler panel to apply the settings below.
rendering.resourceBlockingHint: Block resource types before they hit the network — speeds up rendering at the cost of fidelity. Images and fonts are typically safe to block for SEO crawls; blocking scripts defeats the point of JS rendering.
rendering.screenshotHint: PNG screenshots written to a sidecar folder next to the .seoproject file. Adds ~150–500ms per URL — leave off unless you need them for the visual audit.

performanceBudget.intro: Set per-page performance ceilings. After each crawl, internal HTML pages that exceed any enabled threshold are flagged under the "Over Performance Budget" issue filter. Response time and page size come from the crawl itself; LCP and CLS use PageSpeed Insights data when present. Set any field to 0 to disable that individual check.

perHostUa.intro: Override the User-Agent on a per-host basis. Useful when crawling a mobile subdomain with the mobile-Googlebot UA in the same run as the desktop site, or when a CDN serves a different page based on the requester's UA. The first matching pattern wins; the global User-Agent (Requests tab) is the fallback.

520.name: Web Server Returned an Unknown Error
520.explanation: Cloudflare connected to the origin server but got back an empty, malformed, or unexpected response (e.g. the connection was reset mid-response, the origin returned headers that are too large, or the origin process crashed). It is a catch-all 'something went wrong at the origin' code.
520.cause1: Origin server crashed, restarted, or ran out of workers/memory while serving the request
520.cause2: Origin closed the TCP connection before sending a complete response (often an app-level timeout or OOM kill)
520.cause3: The crawl's request rate overwhelmed the origin's process pool — 520s that appear in bursts under load almost always mean this
520.cause4: Origin returned response headers larger than Cloudflare allows (rare; usually a misconfigured app)
520.todo1: If 520s appear in bursts across many URLs, lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed) — the origin is being overloaded by the crawl
520.todo2: Re-crawl the affected URLs after the crawl finishes (transient 520s often clear on retry — raise Retry Attempts in Settings → Speed)
520.todo3: If only specific URLs 520 consistently, those pages have a server-side bug — flag them to the site owner

521.name: Web Server Is Down
521.explanation: Cloudflare could not open a TCP connection to the origin server — the origin actively refused the connection or is not listening on the expected port.
521.cause1: Origin web server (nginx/Apache/Node/etc.) is stopped or has crashed
521.cause2: Origin's firewall is blocking Cloudflare's IP ranges (a misconfiguration — the origin should allow Cloudflare)
521.cause3: Origin server is overloaded to the point of not accepting new connections
521.todo1: This is an origin-availability problem, not something the crawler can work around — the site is effectively down for these URLs
521.todo2: Re-crawl later; if it persists, the site is broken

522.name: Connection Timed Out
522.explanation: Cloudflare started a TCP handshake with the origin but it never completed within the timeout — the origin accepted the SYN but never replied, or a network device between them dropped the packets.
522.cause1: Origin is severely overloaded (TCP backlog full)
522.cause2: Origin's firewall is silently dropping (not rejecting) Cloudflare's packets
522.cause3: Network/routing issue between Cloudflare and the origin
522.cause4: Under crawl load: the origin's connection table is exhausted by the crawl's parallel requests
522.todo1: Lower Max Concurrency (Settings → Speed) and re-crawl — connection-table exhaustion is the usual cause when this shows up mid-crawl
522.todo2: Retry the affected URLs after the crawl

523.name: Origin Is Unreachable
523.explanation: Cloudflare could not route to the origin server at all — typically a DNS problem in Cloudflare's origin record, or the origin's network is down.
523.cause1: The site's DNS record in Cloudflare points to a wrong / dead IP
523.cause2: Origin's hosting provider has a network outage
523.cause3: BGP / routing failure between Cloudflare and the origin
523.todo1: Nothing the crawler can do — this is an origin DNS/network misconfiguration

524.name: A Timeout Occurred
524.explanation: Cloudflare made a TCP connection to the origin successfully, but the origin did not send a complete HTTP response within Cloudflare's timeout (100 s by default). The origin is alive but too slow on this request.
524.cause1: A slow database query, external API call, or heavy computation on the page
524.cause2: Origin is overloaded — requests are queuing behind a saturated worker pool
524.cause3: Under crawl load: the crawl filled the origin's request queue and this URL waited too long behind it
524.todo1: Lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed) so the origin isn't saturated
524.todo2: Increase Response Timeout (Settings → Crawler) if you want to give genuinely slow pages more time
524.todo3: Retry affected URLs after the crawl

525.name: SSL Handshake Failed
525.explanation: The TLS handshake between Cloudflare and the origin server failed. This is the Cloudflare↔origin leg, not the browser↔Cloudflare leg you see in the address bar — so the site can look fine to a normal visitor and still 525.
525.cause1: Origin's TLS certificate is expired, self-signed, or for the wrong hostname (with Cloudflare in 'Full (strict)' mode)
525.cause2: Origin only supports old TLS versions / cipher suites that Cloudflare rejects
525.cause3: Origin server is overloaded and dropping TLS handshakes
525.todo1: Origin TLS misconfiguration — not something the crawler can change. Check the host's certificate (the TLS Cert rows in URL Details, for HTTPS)

526.name: Invalid SSL Certificate
526.explanation: Cloudflare (in 'Full (strict)' SSL mode) could not validate the origin server's TLS certificate.
526.cause1: Origin certificate is expired, self-signed, or issued for a different hostname
526.cause2: Certificate chain on the origin is incomplete (missing intermediates)
526.todo1: Origin certificate problem — nothing the crawler can do

527.name: Railgun Error (Cloudflare, deprecated)
527.explanation: A connection error in Cloudflare Railgun (a now-retired origin-acceleration product). Effectively obsolete; if you see it the site is on a very old Cloudflare setup.
527.todo1: Nothing actionable from the crawler side

530.name: Cloudflare Error (usually a firewall / WAF block — error 1020)
530.explanation: A 530 is Cloudflare's way of saying "an error happened, see the error 1xxx code in the body". In a crawl context it is almost always 1020 "Access Denied" — a Cloudflare Firewall / WAF / Bot-Fight rule blocked the request. Less commonly it pairs with 1016 (origin DNS error) or other 1xxx codes.
530.cause1: Cloudflare WAF / Firewall Rules / Bot Fight Mode flagged the crawler — by IP, by User-Agent, by request rate, or by missing browser fingerprints
530.cause2: The site has a "managed challenge" the crawler can't solve
530.cause3: (Rarely) an origin DNS error (1016) rather than a block
530.todo1: Set a browser-like User-Agent (Settings → Requests) — the default crawler UA is the #1 trigger
530.todo2: Lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed) — rapid requests from one IP trip rate-based rules
530.todo3: Respect robots.txt and any declared Crawl-delay (Settings → Crawler)
530.todo4: If the site owner is you, allowlist the crawler in Cloudflare; otherwise this site is intentionally blocking automated access

401.name: Unauthorized
401.explanation: The resource requires authentication and none (or invalid) credentials were sent.
401.cause1: Page is behind HTTP Basic/Bearer auth
401.cause2: A session cookie is required and none was sent
401.todo1: Configure credentials in Settings → Authentication if you have them
401.todo2: Use Settings → Cookies → "Accept all" if the site gates content behind a session

403.name: Forbidden
403.explanation: The server understood the request but refuses to serve it. In a crawl this is most often a bot block or a WAF rule rather than a genuine permission issue.
403.cause1: WAF / bot-protection rule triggered by the crawler User-Agent, IP, or request rate
403.cause2: Directory or file genuinely not accessible to anonymous users
403.todo3: If it's site-wide, the site is actively blocking automated access

404.name: Not Found
404.explanation: The server has no resource at this URL.
404.cause2: Page was removed without a redirect
404.todo1: Fix or remove the linking pages — see the Inlinks tab for who links here

408.name: Request Timeout
408.explanation: The server timed out waiting for the request to complete.
408.cause1: Slow network between crawler and server
408.cause2: Server-side connection timeout set very low
408.todo1: Usually transient — raise Retry Attempts (Settings → Speed)

410.name: Gone
410.explanation: The resource was intentionally and permanently removed — stronger than a 404.
410.cause1: Page deliberately retired; the server is telling crawlers to drop it
410.todo1: Remove links to this URL — Google will de-index it faster than a 404

429.name: Too Many Requests (rate limited)
429.explanation: The server is rate-limiting the crawler — too many requests in too short a window from this IP/User-Agent.
429.cause1: Crawl rate exceeds the server's per-client limit
429.todo1: Lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed)
429.todo2: Honour the Retry-After header — see "From the response headers" below if the server sent one

451.name: Unavailable for Legal Reasons
451.explanation: The resource is blocked for legal reasons (court order, GDPR geoblock, DMCA, etc.).

500.name: Internal Server Error
500.explanation: An unhandled error occurred in the server-side application while building the page.
500.cause1: Bug in the page template / backend code
500.todo1: Retry after the crawl (transient 500s clear; persistent ones are a real bug)
500.todo2: If 500s appear under load, the crawl may be overwhelming a database — slow the crawl (Settings → Speed)

502.name: Bad Gateway
502.explanation: A reverse proxy / load balancer in front of the app got an invalid response from the upstream application server.
502.cause1: Upstream app server crashed or returned garbage
502.cause2: Upstream is overloaded — common under crawl load
502.todo1: Lower the crawl rate (Settings → Speed) if 502s appear in bursts
502.todo2: Retry affected URLs after the crawl

503.name: Service Unavailable
503.explanation: The server is temporarily unable to handle the request — usually overload or maintenance. Often comes with a Retry-After header.
503.cause1: Server overloaded — the crawl itself can cause this
503.todo1: Lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed)
503.todo2: Honour Retry-After (see "From the response headers" below)
503.todo3: Retry affected URLs after the crawl

504.name: Gateway Timeout
504.explanation: A reverse proxy / load balancer didn't get a response from the upstream app server in time.
504.cause1: Slow database query / external API call on the page
504.cause3: Under crawl load: the crawl saturated the upstream worker pool
504.todo2: Increase Response Timeout (Settings → Crawler) for genuinely slow pages
504.todo3: Retry affected URLs after the crawl

508.name: Loop Detected
508.explanation: The server detected an infinite loop while processing the request (often WebDAV or a redirect loop server-side).
508.todo1: Server bug — nothing the crawler can do

509.name: Bandwidth Limit Exceeded
509.explanation: A non-standard code (cPanel/Apache) meaning the hosting account hit its monthly bandwidth cap.
509.todo1: Nothing the crawler can do — the host is throttling the whole account

signal.cloudflare: Behind Cloudflare — cf-ray {{ray}}. The status code describes the Cloudflare↔origin link, not what a browser sees.
signal.retryAfterSeconds: Server sent Retry-After: {{seconds}} s — it is explicitly asking clients to back off for that long. A polite crawl should not re-request this URL sooner.
signal.xRobots: X-Robots-Tag: {{value}} — affects indexability regardless of the status.

robots.title: Not Requested — Disallowed by robots.txt
robots.explanation: The crawler never sent a request for this URL: a robots.txt rule for the configured user-agent disallows it. There is no status code because no response was ever asked for — this is not a connection failure.
robots.cause1: A Disallow rule in the site robots.txt matches this path for the crawl user-agent
robots.cause2: The URL is linked from crawled pages, so it is recorded and counted, but never fetched
robots.todo1: Nothing, if the exclusion is intended — Google will not crawl it either
robots.todo2: Check whether the page should be indexable: a disallowed URL cannot pass on link equity and its content is never seen
robots.todo3: Use Help → Robots.txt Tester to see which rule matches, or turn off "Respect robots.txt" in Settings → Crawler to audit it anyway

network.title: No HTTP Response — Network / Connection Error
network.explanationDetail: The request never received an HTTP response. The crawler recorded: "{{detail}}".
network.explanation: The request never received an HTTP response — DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS handshake, or the response read failed before any status line arrived.
network.cause1: DNS could not resolve the hostname (typo, dead domain, or a name only resolvable from inside a private network)
network.cause2: TCP connection refused or timed out (host down, firewall, wrong port)
network.cause3: TLS handshake failed (expired/invalid certificate, protocol mismatch)
network.cause4: Connection reset or read timed out mid-response
network.cause5: Request aborted by the crawler because it exceeded Response Timeout (Settings → Crawler) or Max response time (Settings → Advanced)
network.todo1: Check the hostname resolves and the site is reachable from a normal browser on this machine
network.todo2: If it is reachable but slow, raise Response Timeout (Settings → Crawler)
network.todo3: If it only fails under load, lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s (Settings → Speed) — connection-table exhaustion on the origin looks like a network error to the client
network.todo4: Retry the affected URLs after the crawl (transient resets clear on retry)

informational.title: {{code}} — Informational
informational.explanation: A 1xx response ({{text}}). These are interim responses; the crawler treats them as transient and waits for the final status.

success.explanation: The request succeeded. No diagnosis needed — this section only has extra detail for error and redirect codes.

redirect.explanation301: Permanent redirect. Search engines transfer ranking signals to the target and update their index to the new URL.
redirect.explanation302: Temporary redirect. Search engines keep the original URL indexed. A 302 used long-term is a common SEO mistake — it should usually be a 301.
redirect.explanation308: Permanent redirect (like 301 but the request method is preserved).
redirect.explanation304: Not Modified — the cached copy is still fresh. The crawler normally requests without conditional headers, so this is unusual.
redirect.noLocation: No Location header was captured — unusual for a redirect.
redirect.todoPermanent: If this redirect is permanent, change it to a 301/308 so ranking signals consolidate
redirect.todoChain: Check the Response Codes tab to see the full redirect chain and its final target

clientError.explanation: A 4xx code means the server rejected the request as the client's fault (bad request, not allowed, not found, etc.). In a crawl, persistent 4xx on linked pages usually means broken links; sporadic 4xx can be bot-protection.
clientError.cause3: Method or content the server refuses
clientError.todo1: Check the Inlinks tab to see what links to this URL
clientError.todo2: If it looks like a block, try a browser-like User-Agent and a slower rate (Settings → Requests / Speed)

serverError.explanation: A 5xx code means the server failed to fulfil a request it accepted as valid. Under crawl load these are frequently the crawl overwhelming the origin rather than a genuine page bug.
serverError.cause2: Origin overloaded — possibly by the crawl itself
serverError.todo1: Lower Max Concurrency / Max URL/s and add a Per-Worker Delay (Settings → Speed) if 5xx appear in bursts
serverError.todo2: Raise Retry Attempts (Settings → Speed) and re-crawl affected URLs

Reset ALL crawl settings to their defaults?

This clears include/exclude patterns, custom search & extraction rules, URL rewrites, auth, proxy profiles, per-host user-agents, and webhook URL. Nothing is saved until you click Save — Cancel still discards.

language.title: Language
language.intro: Select the UI display language. Applied immediately.
language.label: UI language
language.note: Some deep panels and dialogs may still display English while broader coverage is being added.

spelling.title: Spelling
spelling.intro: Spelling, grammar and style checks run through LanguageTool against pages you select in the Spelling tab. Each page's language is detected from its own text and cross-checked against html[lang]; pages in a language LanguageTool has no rules for are reported as unsupported rather than graded against the wrong dictionary. Configure the endpoint (public API or self-hosted) under Integrations → LanguageTool.
spelling.levelDefault: Default — spelling and grammar errors only
spelling.levelPicky: Picky — also flags style, typography and wordiness
spelling.dictionaryHint: Words to never flag — brand names, product names, industry jargon. One per line, or separated by commas. Case-insensitive.
spelling.languageHint: Leave on auto unless detection gets a site wrong. Pinning a language forces every page to be checked in it — useful for a single-language site whose html[lang] is wrong, and it also turns off the safety check that discards implausibly noisy results.
spelling.languageAuto: Auto — detect from each page's text (recommended)

storage.title: Storage
storage.intro: Default folder for new .seoproject files. Save As dialogs open here by default; the Open dialog is not constrained.
storage.modeDisk: Disk (SQLite file) — persistent, resumable, uses worker pools
storage.modeRam: RAM-only (in-memory) — fastest, nothing written to disk until Save As
storage.modeRestart: Applies the next time FreeCrawl starts (currently running in {{active}} mode).
storage.modeRamWarning: In-memory projects are lost on exit — and when you open or switch to another project — unless you Save As first. Crash recovery is off and very large crawls are bounded by available RAM.
storage.resetTitle: Reset to the OS Documents folder
storage.note: Active crawl data lives in the app's user-data directory until you Save As — the path above only controls where Save As starts. Changing this won't move any existing project files.
storage.autoSaveLabel: Auto-save project every N crawled URLs — 0 = off
storage.autoSaveHint: While a crawl runs, the open .seoproject file is rewritten each time this many more URLs have been crawled, so a crash or power loss costs at most one batch. Only applies once the project has been saved to a file; minimum {{min}}. Each save is a full snapshot, so keep it in the thousands on large sites.

agents.title: Agent Sessions (MCP)
agents.intro: AI agents can open their own isolated crawl sessions inside this app over MCP. These limits keep several parallel agents from oversubscribing the machine.
agents.note: An idle session with a saved project is saved before it is closed. Changes apply to sessions created from now on.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.intro: FreeCrawl is local-first — crawl results, project files, and URLs you visit never leave your machine.
privacy.telemetryHelp: Off by default. When on, aggregated counts of feature use (e.g. "export ran", "report opened") may be sent — never URLs, project contents, or crawl results.
privacy.statusNote: No telemetry endpoint is currently wired up. Toggling this preference is recorded but nothing is transmitted in the current build. The toggle is exposed now so consent state persists across upgrades when a future build adds an endpoint.

mcp.intro: Connect external MCP servers so the Assistant tab can use their tools alongside your crawl data. Local servers run as a child process; remote ones are called over HTTP. Every tool call asks for your approval the first time.
mcp.empty: No servers yet. A typical local server looks like: command "npx", arguments "-y" and "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", plus any API key as an environment variable.

mcp.argsHint: One per line. Passed as a vector — no shell, so quotes and spaces are literal.
mcp.envHint: KEY=value per line. Values are stored encrypted with your OS keychain and shown masked.
mcp.headersHint: Name: value per line. Stored encrypted and shown masked.
